question_html: Under section 2(31) of the Companies Act, 2013, how is the term 'deposit' defined?

options.A: It is an inclusive definition, covering any receipt of money by way of deposit or loan or in any other form by a company, but excluding such categories of amount as may be prescribed in consultation with the Reserve Bank of India
options.B: It is an exhaustive definition, covering only money received strictly by way of a formal fixed deposit receipt, and excluding any loan or other form of receipt
options.C: It is an inclusive definition covering every receipt of money by a company without exception, with no power to prescribe excluded categories at all
options.D: It is an exhaustive definition confined to money received from the company's own members, with all receipts from non-members automatically falling outside its scope

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) It is an inclusive definition, covering any receipt of money by way of deposit or loan or in any other form by a company, but excluding such categories of amount as may be prescribed in consultation with the Reserve Bank of India

Section 2(31) defines 'deposit' inclusively, as any receipt of money by way of deposit or loan or in any other form by a company - but expressly excludes such categories of amount as may be prescribed in consultation with the Reserve Bank of India (these excluded categories are set out in Rule 2(1)(c) of the Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Rules, 2014).

question_html: Among the key features of 'deposit' recognised under Chapter V, which of the following correctly describes the security and joint-holding characteristics of a deposit?

options.A: A deposit must always be fully secured by a charge on the company's assets, whether tangible or intangible, and can never be accepted in joint names
options.B: A deposit can be secured (fully secured by creating a charge on tangible assets) or unsecured (with partial or no security made available), and it may be accepted by the company in joint names not exceeding three persons
options.C: A deposit can only ever be unsecured, since the Act does not permit a company to create any charge in favour of depositors, and may be accepted in joint names of any number of persons
options.D: A deposit can be secured or unsecured, but the Act limits its acceptance strictly to a single depositor's own individual name, with no provision for joint holding

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) A deposit can be secured (fully secured by creating a charge on tangible assets) or unsecured (with partial or no security made available), and it may be accepted by the company in joint names not exceeding three persons

Deposits may be secured (fully secured by a charge on tangible assets) or unsecured (partial or no security). A deposit may be accepted by the company in joint names not exceeding three persons, and a depositor may nominate any person at any time.

question_html: As a key feature distinguishing a private company from a public company under the deposit provisions, from whom may each accept deposits?

options.A: Both a private company and a public company can accept deposits from the public at large without any distinction or additional qualifying parameters
options.B: A private company can accept deposits from the public at large, whereas a public company is restricted to accepting deposits from its own members only
options.C: A private company can accept deposits from its members only, whereas a public company can accept deposits from its members and, if it fulfils certain parameters (i.e., qualifies as an 'eligible company'), also from the public

question_html: Under Rule 2(1)(c)(i), an amount received by a company from which of the following sources is NOT considered as a deposit?

options.A: Any private unlisted company, regardless of whether repayment is guaranteed by the Central or State Government
options.B: Any individual resident in India who is not a relative of a director of the company, regardless of any government guarantee
options.C: Any co-operative society other than a co-operative bank, regardless of whether repayment is guaranteed by the Central or State Government

question_html: Under Rule 2(1)(c)(ii), amounts received from foreign Governments, foreign or international banks, multilateral financial institutions, foreign export credit agencies, foreign collaborators, or foreign bodies corporate/citizens are excluded from 'deposit' - subject to what overarching condition?

question_html: Which of the following amounts is correctly excluded from the meaning of 'deposit' under Rule 2(1)(c)(iii), (iv), and (vi)?

options.A: A loan received from any unincorporated body of individuals carrying on a private money-lending business, regardless of whether it is registered with the Reserve Bank of India
options.B: A loan or facility received from any banking company, the State Bank of India or its subsidiary banks, a notified banking institution, or any co-operative bank; a loan or financial assistance from Public Financial Institutions, regional financial institutions, insurance companies, or scheduled banks; and any amount received by a company from any other company (an Inter Company Deposit)
options.C: A loan received from any individual shareholder of the company who is not a director, regardless of the source of his own funds
options.D: An amount received from any other company only where that other company is the holding company of the recipient company, this being the sole basis on which an Inter Company Deposit is excluded

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) A loan or facility received from any banking company, the State Bank of India or its subsidiary banks, a notified banking institution, or any co-operative bank; a loan or financial assistance from Public Financial Institutions, regional financial institutions, insurance companies, or scheduled banks; and any amount received by a company from any other company (an Inter Company Deposit)

Rule 2(1)(c)(iii) excludes loans/facilities from banking companies, SBI/its subsidiaries, notified banking institutions, and co-operative banks. Rule 2(1)(c)(iv) excludes loans/financial assistance from Public Financial Institutions, regional financial institutions, insurance companies, and scheduled banks. Rule 2(1)(c)(vi) excludes any amount received by a company from any other company (commonly known as an Inter Company Deposit or ICD), with no requirement of a holding-subsidiary relationship.

question_html: Under Rule 2(1)(c)(vii) and the Explanation thereto, an amount received and held towards subscription to securities (including share application money) is excluded from 'deposit' so long as it is appropriated only against the amount due on allotment - but under what circumstance does such an amount become deemed to be a deposit?

options.A: If the securities cannot be allotted within 30 days from the date of receipt of the application money, regardless of whether any refund is subsequently made
options.B: If the company adjusts the amount for any purpose other than allotment or refund, such adjustment is itself treated as a valid refund and the amount never becomes a deposit
options.C: If the securities cannot be allotted within 60 days from the date of receipt of the application money/advance, and such amount is not refunded to the subscribers within 15 days from the date of completion of those 60 days, the amount shall be treated as a deposit
options.D: If the aggregate application money received from all subscribers in a financial year exceeds rupees one crore, regardless of the allotment timeline

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) If the securities cannot be allotted within 60 days from the date of receipt of the application money/advance, and such amount is not refunded to the subscribers within 15 days from the date of completion of those 60 days, the amount shall be treated as a deposit

The Explanation to Rule 2(1)(c)(vii) clarifies that if securities cannot be allotted within 60 days of receipt of the application money/advance, and such money is not refunded within 15 days from completion of those 60 days, the amount is treated as a deposit. It is further clarified that any adjustment of the amount for any OTHER purpose shall not be treated as a refund.

question_html: Under Rule 2(1)(c)(viii), an amount received from a person who was, at the time of receipt, a director of the company (or a relative of the director of a PRIVATE company) is excluded from 'deposit', subject to what conditions?

options.A: No declaration or disclosure of any kind is required; the exclusion applies automatically and unconditionally to any amount received from a director or any relative of a director of any company, public or private
options.B: The director or relative must obtain prior approval of the Reserve Bank of India before advancing the amount, and the company need not disclose the amount anywhere in its financial statements or Board's report
options.C: The exclusion applies only where the amount is routed through a scheduled bank account and is accompanied by an affidavit sworn before a magistrate, with no requirement for Board's report disclosure
options.D: The director or relative (as the case may be) must furnish to the company, at the time of giving the money, a written declaration that the amount is not being given out of funds acquired by him by borrowing or accepting loans or deposits from others, and the company must disclose the details of the money so accepted in its Board's report

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) The director or relative (as the case may be) must furnish to the company, at the time of giving the money, a written declaration that the amount is not being given out of funds acquired by him by borrowing or accepting loans or deposits from others, and the company must disclose the details of the money so accepted in its Board's report

Rule 2(1)(c)(viii) requires the director (of any company) or relative of the director (of a PRIVATE company only) giving the money to furnish a written declaration, at the time of giving the money, that it is not sourced from funds he himself borrowed or accepted as loans/deposits - and the company must disclose the details of money so accepted in its Board's report. Note that for a relative's amount to qualify, the recipient must specifically be a private company.

question_html: A company receives share application money on 1st March. If the securities applied for are not allotted, by when must the company allot the securities to avoid the amount being treated as a deposit at all, and, failing allotment, by when must it refund the money to avoid the deeming provision under Rule 2(1)(c)(vii) applying?

options.A: The securities should ordinarily be allotted within 60 days of receipt of the application money (i.e., by around 30th April); if not allotted, the amount must be refunded within 15 days from the date of completion of those 60 days (i.e., by around 15th May) to avoid the amount being deemed a deposit
options.B: The securities must be allotted within 30 days of receipt of the application money, and if not allotted, refunded within a further 30 days, i.e., within 60 days in total from the date of receipt
options.C: There is no time limit at all for allotment or refund of share application money under Rule 2(1)(c)(vii); the exclusion from 'deposit' continues indefinitely regardless of delay
options.D: The securities must be allotted within 90 days of receipt of the application money, and if not allotted, refunded within 6 months from the date of receipt, to avoid the deeming provision applying

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) The securities should ordinarily be allotted within 60 days of receipt of the application money (i.e., by around 30th April); if not allotted, the amount must be refunded within 15 days from the date of completion of those 60 days (i.e., by around 15th May) to avoid the amount being deemed a deposit

Per the Explanation to Rule 2(1)(c)(vii): if securities are not allotted within 60 days from receipt of the application money, and the amount is not refunded within a further 15 days from completion of that 60-day period, the amount is treated as a deposit - i.e., the outer limit for the money to remain outside 'deposit' is 60 + 15 = 75 days from the date of receipt, absent allotment.

options.A: Where the bonds/debentures are secured by a charge on the company's intangible assets alone, such as goodwill or trademarks, regardless of any registered valuer's assessment

question_html: Under Rule 2(1)(c)(xiii), an unsecured loan brought in by the promoters of a company (pursuant to a stipulation of a lending financial institution or bank) is excluded from 'deposit' subject to which conditions?

options.B: The loan must be provided exclusively by the promoters personally (never by their relatives), and the exemption is available only for a fixed period of five years from the date the loan is brought in, regardless of repayment status

question_html: Under Rule 2(1)(c)(xvii), an amount of Rs. 25 lakh or more received by a start-up company by way of a convertible note is excluded from 'deposit' only if received in what manner?

question_html: Applying the rule that the circular to members remains valid till the earliest of two dates, if Ray Pharmaceuticals Limited issues a circular on 14-02-2025 and its AGM (for FY 2024-25) is held on 07-09-2025, until what date does the circular remain valid?

options.A: 30-09-2025 - since this is exactly six months from the closure of FY 2024-25, and the rule always applies the later, not the earlier, of the two possible dates
options.B: 07-09-2025 - since the AGM date (07-09-2025) is earlier than the date six months from closure of FY 2024-25 (which would be 30-09-2025), the circular's validity ends on the earlier of the two dates, i.e., the AGM date

answer_html:

question_html: Under Rule 3(1), within what tenure band must deposits accepted or renewed by a company ordinarily fall, and what illustrative repayment window applies where a member deposits money on 1st April, 2025?

options.B: A company can accept deposits repayable on demand at any time, subject only to an outer maximum tenure of 24 months from the date of acceptance

question_html: Under section 76(1), a public company may accept deposits from persons other than its members (thereby qualifying as an 'eligible company') if it satisfies which financial criterion?

options.A: It has a net worth of not less than Rs. 500 crore AND a turnover of not less than Rs. 100 crore, both criteria being cumulatively mandatory

question_html: Under Rule 6, a company accepting secured deposits from the public must create security within what time period, and on what category of assets alone?

options.A: Within 30 days of such acceptance, by way of charge on the company's TANGIBLE assets only (a charge cannot be created on intangible assets such as goodwill or trademarks), with the total value of security not less than the amount of deposits accepted plus interest payable thereon, as assessed by a registered valuer
options.B: Within 90 days of such acceptance, by way of charge on either tangible or intangible assets at the company's discretion, with no minimum value threshold prescribed for the security
options.C: Within 30 days of such acceptance, by way of charge on the company's intangible assets exclusively (such as goodwill and trademarks), since tangible assets are reserved as security for secured creditors and debenture-holders
options.D: Within 15 days of such acceptance, by way of charge on any assets of the company, tangible or intangible, with the total value of security capped at exactly the amount of deposits accepted (excluding any interest component)

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Within 30 days of such acceptance, by way of charge on the company's TANGIBLE assets only (a charge cannot be created on intangible assets such as goodwill or trademarks), with the total value of security not less than the amount of deposits accepted plus interest payable thereon, as assessed by a registered valuer

question_html: Under Rule 3(4), what are the respective ceilings on deposits an eligible company may accept (including outstanding deposits) from its members, and from persons other than its members?

options.A: From members: not exceeding 25% of the aggregate; from persons other than members: not exceeding 10% of the aggregate - i.e., the reverse of the correct allocation
options.B: From members: the deposit (together with outstanding member deposits) shall not exceed 10% of the aggregate of paid-up share capital, free reserves, and securities premium account; from persons other than members: the deposit (together with outstanding non-member deposits) shall not exceed 25% of that same aggregate
options.C: From members: not exceeding 35% of the aggregate (the same ceiling as an ordinary, non-eligible company); from persons other than members: not exceeding 50% of that aggregate
options.D: There is no distinction between member and non-member deposits for an eligible company; both are subject to a uniform ceiling of 25% of the aggregate

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) From members: the deposit (together with outstanding member deposits) shall not exceed 10% of the aggregate of paid-up share capital, free reserves, and securities premium account; from persons other than members: the deposit (together with outstanding non-member deposits) shall not exceed 25% of that same aggregate

Rule 3(4) caps an eligible company's deposits from members (plus outstanding member deposits) at 10% of the aggregate of paid-up share capital, free reserves, and securities premium account, and its deposits from non-members (plus outstanding non-member deposits) at 25% of that same aggregate - a lower member-specific ceiling than the 35% applicable to an ordinary company under Rule 3(3).

question_html: Under section 76A, where a company contravenes the manner or conditions prescribed under section 73 or section 76 (or fails to repay deposits within the specified/extended time), what punishment is prescribed for the company and for the officer-in-default?

options.A: The company shall be punishable with a fine not less than Rs. 10 crore in every case, with no reference to the amount of deposit accepted, and the officer-in-default faces only a fine, with no provision for imprisonment under section 76A
options.B: The company shall be punishable with a fine not less than Rs. 1 crore or twice the deposit amount, whichever is HIGHER, extendable to Rs. 25 crore, and the officer-in-default faces imprisonment extendable to 3 years only
options.C: The company faces no monetary fine under section 76A at all, its sole obligation being repayment of the deposit and interest, while the officer-in-default alone is punishable with imprisonment and fine
options.D: The company shall, in addition to repaying the deposit and interest due, be punishable with a fine not less than Rs. 1 crore or twice the amount of deposit accepted (whichever is LOWER), extendable to Rs. 10 crore; every officer-in-default shall be punishable with imprisonment extendable to 7 years and a fine of not less than Rs. 25 lakh but extendable to Rs. 2 crore

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) The company shall, in addition to repaying the deposit and interest due, be punishable with a fine not less than Rs. 1 crore or twice the amount of deposit accepted (whichever is LOWER), extendable to Rs. 10 crore; every officer-in-default shall be punishable with imprisonment extendable to 7 years and a fine of not less than Rs. 25 lakh but extendable to Rs. 2 crore

question_html: Under section 74(1), where a deposit was accepted by a company before 1st April, 2014 and remains unpaid (wholly or partly) on or after that date, what must the company do?

options.A: It must file, within 3 months from the commencement of the Act (or from the date such payment becomes due), a statement of all deposits accepted and sums remaining unpaid (with interest payable) along with the repayment arrangements, with the Registrar; and it must repay the deposit within 3 years from such commencement, or on/before expiry of the period for which the deposit was accepted, whichever is EARLIER
options.B: It must file the statement within 6 months of commencement, and repay the deposit within 5 years from commencement or the original expiry period, whichever is LATER
options.C: It has no obligation to file any statement with the Registrar at all, provided it repays the deposit within 10 years of commencement of the Act
options.D: It must file the statement within 1 month of commencement, and repay the deposit within 1 year from commencement, with no reference at all to the original tenure for which the deposit was accepted

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) It must file, within 3 months from the commencement of the Act (or from the date such payment becomes due), a statement of all deposits accepted and sums remaining unpaid (with interest payable) along with the repayment arrangements, with the Registrar; and it must repay the deposit within 3 years from such commencement, or on/before expiry of the period for which the deposit was accepted, whichever is EARLIER

Section 74(1) requires filing (within 3 months of commencement, or of the payment falling due) of a statement of unpaid pre-Act deposits with the Registrar, and repayment within 3 years of commencement OR expiry of the original deposit period, whichever is EARLIER - though per the Explanation to Rule 19, continuing timely repayment without default in accordance with the original terms is deemed compliance with the repayment limb.

question_html: Which of the following correctly states the consequences applicable where a company fails to repay deposits on maturity, or contravenes a deposit rule for which no specific punishment is otherwise provided?

options.A: The penal rate of interest for overdue deposits is 12% per annum, the Tribunal has no power to extend the repayment time for pre-2013-Act deposits under any circumstances, and there is no general 'catch-all' penalty for contraventions lacking a specific punishment provision
options.B: The company must pay a penal rate of interest of 18% per annum for the overdue period; the Tribunal may, on the company's application (under section 74(2)), allow further reasonable time to repay pre-2013-Act deposits after considering the company's financial condition; and for a rule contravention with no separate punishment prescribed, the company and every officer-in-default are punishable with a fine extendable to Rs. 5,000 (plus a further fine up to Rs. 500 per day for a continuing contravention)
options.C: The penal rate of interest for overdue deposits is 24% per annum, the Tribunal's extension power under section 74(2) applies only to post-2013-Act deposits, and the general contravention fine is a flat Rs. 50,000 with no continuing-default component
options.D: The penal rate of interest for overdue deposits is 18% per annum, but the Tribunal's extension power under section 74(2) is available only once in the company's lifetime, and the general contravention fine is capped at Rs. 1,000 in total, regardless of the duration of the continuing default

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) The company must pay a penal rate of interest of 18% per annum for the overdue period; the Tribunal may, on the company's application (under section 74(2)), allow further reasonable time to repay pre-2013-Act deposits after considering the company's financial condition; and for a rule contravention with no separate punishment prescribed, the company and every officer-in-default are punishable with a fine extendable to Rs. 5,000 (plus a further fine up to Rs. 500 per day for a continuing contravention)

Rule 17 prescribes 18% p.a. penal interest for the overdue period on unpaid matured deposits. Section 74(2) empowers the Tribunal, on the company's application, to allow further reasonable time for repayment of pre-2013-Act deposits, having regard to its financial condition and the deposit/interest amount. case_facts_html: Alacrity Renewables Private Limited, a company recognised as a 'start-up' under the applicable Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade notification, receives the following amounts in a financial year: (i) Rs. 15 lakh from Investor Priyank on 5th June and a further Rs. 12 lakh from the same Investor Priyank on 20th September, both by way of convertible notes repayable within 8 years from the date of issue, or convertible into equity shares; (ii) Rs. 4 lakh from Mr. Ishaan, who is a relative of one of Alacrity's directors, accompanied by a written declaration from Mr. Ishaan (furnished at the time of giving the money) that the amount is not sourced from any funds borrowed by him from others; and (iii) Rs. 5,50,000 received as a non-interest bearing security deposit under a contract of employment from Ms. Meher, an employee of Alacrity drawing an annual salary of Rs. 5,00,000.
question_html:
Alacrity Renewables Private Limited, a company recognised as a 'start-up' under the applicable Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade notification, receives the following amounts in a financial year: (i) Rs. 15 lakh from Investor Priyank on 5th June and a further Rs. 12 lakh from the same Investor Priyank on 20th September, both by way of convertible notes repayable within 8 years from the date of issue, or convertible into equity shares; (ii) Rs. 4 lakh from Mr. Ishaan, who is a relative of one of Alacrity's directors, accompanied by a written declaration from Mr. Ishaan (furnished at the time of giving the money) that the amount is not sourced from any funds borrowed by him from others; and (iii) Rs. 5,50,000 received as a non-interest bearing security deposit under a contract of employment from Ms. Meher, an employee of Alacrity drawing an annual salary of Rs. 5,00,000.

Are the amounts received by Alacrity Renewables from Investor Priyank (Rs. 15 lakh and Rs. 12 lakh, aggregating Rs. 27 lakh) excluded from 'deposit' under Rule 2(1)(c)(xvii)?

options.A: Yes - since the aggregate amount of Rs. 27 lakh exceeds Rs. 25 lakh and the notes are repayable within 10 years, the single-tranche requirement is a mere formality that does not affect the exclusion
options.B: No - because Rs. 27 lakh exceeds the absolute statutory ceiling of Rs. 25 lakh for start-up convertible notes, any amount above that ceiling is automatically treated as a deposit regardless of how it was tranched
options.C: No - although the aggregate of Rs. 27 lakh exceeds the Rs. 25 lakh threshold and the notes are convertible/repayable within the permitted 10-year window, Rule 2(1)(c)(xvii) requires the amount to be received in a SINGLE TRANCHE from a person; since the two amounts were received on different dates (5th June and 20th September), they were not received in a single tranche, and the amounts are therefore treated as a deposit - directly analogous to the Greedwood Limited illustration
options.D: Yes - because the money was received entirely from a single investor (Priyank), the 'single tranche' requirement is satisfied irrespective of the number of separate dates on which amounts were received

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) No - although the aggregate of Rs. 27 lakh exceeds the Rs. 25 lakh threshold and the notes are convertible/repayable within the permitted 10-year window, Rule 2(1)(c)(xvii) requires the amount to be received in a SINGLE TRANCHE from a person; since the two amounts were received on different dates (5th June and 20th September), they were not received in a single tranche, and the amounts are therefore treated as a deposit - directly analogous to the Greedwood Limited illustration

Rule 2(1)(c)(xvii) excludes Rs. 25 lakh or more received by a start-up as a convertible note ONLY if received in a single tranche from a person. Receiving Rs. 15 lakh and Rs. 12 lakh on different dates from the same investor does not satisfy the single-tranche requirement (as with Greedwood Limited's Rs. 20 lakh and Rs. 10 lakh received on different dates), so the amounts are treated as a deposit despite exceeding Rs. 25 lakh in aggregate and being within the 10-year conversion/repayment window.

Alacrity Renewables Private Limited, a company recognised as a 'start-up' under the applicable Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade notification, receives the following amounts in a financial year: (i) Rs. 15 lakh from Investor Priyank on 5th June and a further Rs. 12 lakh from the same Investor Priyank on 20th September, both by way of convertible notes repayable within 8 years from the date of issue, or convertible into equity shares; (ii) Rs. 4 lakh from Mr. Ishaan, who is a relative of one of Alacrity's directors, accompanied by a written declaration from Mr. Ishaan (furnished at the time of giving the money) that the amount is not sourced from any funds borrowed by him from others; and (iii) Rs. 5,50,000 received as a non-interest bearing security deposit under a contract of employment from Ms. Meher, an employee of Alacrity drawing an annual salary of Rs. 5,00,000.

Is the Rs. 4 lakh received from Mr. Ishaan (a relative of a director) excluded from 'deposit' under Rule 2(1)(c)(viii)?

options.A: No - Rule 2(1)(c)(viii) excludes amounts from a relative of a director only where the recipient is a PUBLIC company, and Alacrity, being a private company, cannot avail this exclusion regardless of any declaration furnished
options.B: No - a written declaration from the relative is not sufficient by itself; the exclusion additionally requires prior approval of the Reserve Bank of India, which has not been obtained here
options.C: Yes - the exclusion applies to amounts from a relative of a director of any company, public or private, with no declaration or Board's report disclosure required at all
options.D: Yes - since Alacrity Renewables is a PRIVATE company, an amount received from a relative of a director is excluded from 'deposit' provided the relative furnishes, at the time of giving the money, a written declaration that the amount is not sourced from funds he himself borrowed or accepted as loans/deposits from others; Mr. Ishaan has furnished such a declaration, so the exclusion applies (the company must also disclose the amount in its Board's report)

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) Yes - since Alacrity Renewables is a PRIVATE company, an amount received from a relative of a director is excluded from 'deposit' provided the relative furnishes, at the time of giving the money, a written declaration that the amount is not sourced from funds he himself borrowed or accepted as loans/deposits from others; Mr. Ishaan has furnished such a declaration, so the exclusion applies (the company must also disclose the amount in its Board's report)

Alacrity being private and the declaration having been furnished, the Rs. 4 lakh is excluded from 'deposit'.

case_facts_html: Kavach Software Private Limited is not an associate or subsidiary company of any other company. Its borrowings from banks and financial institutions total Rs. 15 lakh, which is less than both twice its paid-up share capital (Rs. 40 lakh, i.e., twice is Rs. 80 lakh) and Rs. 50 crore, and it has not defaulted in repayment of any such borrowings subsisting at the time of accepting deposits. The aggregate of Kavach's paid-up share capital, free reserves, and securities premium account is Rs. 90 lakh. The company proposes to accept Rs. 85 lakh in deposits from its members, without issuing the circular under section 73(2)(a), without filing any circular with the Registrar under section 73(2)(b), and without creating a Deposit Repayment Reserve Account under section 73(2)(c).
question_html:
Kavach Software Private Limited is not an associate or subsidiary company of any other company. Its borrowings from banks and financial institutions total Rs. 15 lakh, which is less than both twice its paid-up share capital (Rs. 40 lakh, i.e., twice is Rs. 80 lakh) and Rs. 50 crore, and it has not defaulted in repayment of any such borrowings subsisting at the time of accepting deposits. The aggregate of Kavach's paid-up share capital, free reserves, and securities premium account is Rs. 90 lakh. The company proposes to accept Rs. 85 lakh in deposits from its members, without issuing the circular under section 73(2)(a), without filing any circular with the Registrar under section 73(2)(b), and without creating a Deposit Repayment Reserve Account under section 73(2)(c).

Is Kavach Software Private Limited correct in dispensing with the circular, Registrar-filing, and Deposit Repayment Reserve Account requirements of clauses (a) to (c) of section 73(2)?

options.A: No - the exemption from clauses (a) to (e) of section 73(2) is available only to private companies that are start-ups, and Kavach, not being a start-up, cannot claim this exemption regardless of its borrowing/default profile
options.B: Yes - since Kavach fulfils all three conditions of category (C) of the exemption (not an associate/subsidiary of any other company; borrowings from banks/financial institutions less than the LOWER of twice its paid-up share capital or Rs. 50 crore; and no default in repayment of such borrowings), clauses (a) to (e) of section 73(2) - covering the circular, Registrar filing, Deposit Repayment Reserve Account, and certification requirements - do not apply to it
options.C: No - the exemption requires the company's aggregate paid-up capital, free reserves, and securities premium account to exceed Rs. 100 crore, which Kavach (at Rs. 90 lakh) does not meet
options.D: Yes, but only for a period of five years from Kavach's date of incorporation, this exemption category being time-limited in the same manner as the start-up exemption

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) Yes - since Kavach fulfils all three conditions of category (C) of the exemption (not an associate/subsidiary of any other company; borrowings from banks/financial institutions less than the LOWER of twice its paid-up share capital or Rs. 50 crore; and no default in repayment of such borrowings), clauses (a) to (e) of section 73(2) - covering the circular, Registrar filing, Deposit Repayment Reserve Account, and certification requirements - do not apply to it

The exemption from clauses (a) to (e) of section 73(2) is available (among other routes) to a private company satisfying ALL of: not being an associate/subsidiary of any other company; borrowings from banks/FIs/body corporates being less than the LOWER of 2x paid-up share capital or Rs. 50 crore; and no default on such borrowings. Kavach satisfies all three conditions (borrowings of Rs. 15 lakh being well below the lower of Rs. 80 lakh and Rs. 50 crore), so it validly qualifies for this exemption - it is not confined to start-ups, and there is no separate net-worth threshold under this route.

options.A: No - Kavach is bound by the general 35% ceiling applicable to an ordinary company under Rule 3(3), i.e., a maximum of Rs. 31.5 lakh (35% of Rs. 90 lakh), so the proposed Rs. 85 lakh acceptance is impermissible
options.B: No - even a qualifying private company is capped at 75% of the aggregate under Rule 3(3), i.e., a maximum of Rs. 67.5 lakh, so the proposed Rs. 85 lakh acceptance exceeds this enhanced but still-capped limit
options.C: Yes - since Kavach meets the same category-(C) conditions that also exempt it from the general 35% ceiling under Rule 3(3), it may accept deposits from members up to 100% of the Rs. 90 lakh aggregate (i.e., up to Rs. 90 lakh); Rs. 85 lakh is within this enhanced 100% limit
options.D: Yes, but only if Kavach additionally obtains the prior approval of the Reserve Bank of India before accepting any amount above the ordinary 35% ceiling

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Yes - since Kavach meets the same category-(C) conditions that also exempt it from the general 35% ceiling under Rule 3(3), it may accept deposits from members up to 100% of the Rs. 90 lakh aggregate (i.e., up to Rs. 90 lakh); Rs. 85 lakh is within this enhanced 100% limit

It proposes to invite deposits from the public amounting to Rs. 20 crore, which falls within the limits specified under section 180(1)(c). question_html:
Vantage Industries Limited, a public company, has a net worth of Rs. 150 crore and a turnover of Rs. 300 crore. It proposes to invite deposits from the public amounting to Rs. 20 crore, which falls within the limits specified under section 180(1)(c). Vantage obtained a credit rating (covering its net-worth, liquidity, and ability to pay deposits on the due date) from a recognised credit rating agency at the time it first invited public deposits three years ago, and has not obtained any fresh rating since.

Does Vantage Industries Limited qualify as an 'eligible company' under Rule 2(1)(e), given its net worth of Rs. 150 crore and turnover of Rs. 300 crore?

options.A: Yes - Rule 2(1)(e) requires a public company to have EITHER a net worth of not less than Rs. 100 crore OR a turnover of not less than Rs. 500 crore; Vantage's net worth of Rs. 150 crore independently satisfies the net-worth limb (even though its turnover of Rs. 300 crore falls short of the Rs. 500 crore turnover limb), so it qualifies as an eligible company
options.B: No - Rule 2(1)(e) requires BOTH the net worth and turnover criteria to be satisfied simultaneously, and since Vantage's turnover (Rs. 300 crore) is below Rs. 500 crore, it fails to qualify as an eligible company despite its net worth
options.C: No - Vantage's net worth of Rs. 150 crore is below the Rs. 500 crore threshold applicable to net worth (with Rs. 100 crore applying only to turnover), so it does not qualify as an eligible company
options.D: Yes, but only because its turnover of Rs. 300 crore independently exceeds the Rs. 100 crore net-worth threshold; net worth itself is not a relevant criterion under Rule 2(1)(e)

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Yes - Rule 2(1)(e) requires a public company to have EITHER a net worth of not less than Rs. 100 crore OR a turnover of not less than Rs. 500 crore; Vantage's net worth of Rs. 150 crore independently satisfies the net-worth limb (even though its turnover of Rs. 300 crore falls short of the Rs. 500 crore turnover limb), so it qualifies as an eligible company

Rule 2(1)(e) sets out two ALTERNATIVE financial criteria - net worth of at least Rs. 100 crore OR turnover of at least Rs. 500 crore - either of which independently qualifies a public company as an 'eligible company'. Vantage's net worth of Rs. 150 crore satisfies the net-worth limb on its own, so it qualifies regardless of its turnover falling short of Rs. 500 crore.

Vantage Industries Limited, a public company, has a net worth of Rs. 150 crore and a turnover of Rs. 300 crore. Since Vantage's proposed public deposit of Rs. 20 crore falls within the limits specified under section 180(1)(c), what resolution must it pass to authorise this invitation of public deposits?

options.A: A special resolution is mandatorily required in every case, irrespective of whether the deposit amount falls within or outside the section 180(1)(c) limits, since the proviso applies only to private companies
options.B: An ordinary resolution suffices, by virtue of the first proviso to section 76(1) (also reflected in the proviso to Rule 2(1)(e)), which dispenses with the special-resolution requirement where the eligible company's deposit acceptance falls within the section 180(1)(c) limits
options.C: No resolution of any kind is required where the deposit amount falls within the section 180(1)(c) limits; only Board-level authorisation is necessary
options.D: A special resolution passed by postal ballot alone (and not at a physical or hybrid general meeting) is required, since public deposits inherently require the heightened postal-ballot procedure

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) An ordinary resolution suffices, by virtue of the first proviso to section 76(1) (also reflected in the proviso to Rule 2(1)(e)), which dispenses with the special-resolution requirement where the eligible company's deposit acceptance falls within the section 180(1)(c) limits

The first proviso to section 76(1) allows an eligible company to accept deposits within section 180(1)(c) limits by ordinary resolution, dispensing with the otherwise-mandatory special resolution - Vantage's Rs. 20 crore invitation, being within those limits, may therefore be authorised by ordinary resolution.

Is Vantage Industries Limited compliant with the credit rating requirement, having obtained a rating only once, three years ago, at the time of its first public deposit invitation?

options.A: Yes - the credit rating requirement under section 76(1) is a one-time obligation triggered only at the time of the company's first-ever invitation of public deposits, with no obligation to renew it in subsequent years
options.B: Yes - since Vantage's net worth (Rs. 150 crore) exceeds the Rs. 100 crore threshold, it is exempted from the annual credit rating renewal requirement that applies to companies qualifying solely on the turnover criterion

options.D: No, but only because three years have elapsed since the last rating; a company would remain compliant if it renewed its rating once every two years instead of annually

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) No - the second proviso to section 76(1) requires the credit rating to be obtained EVERY YEAR during the tenure of the deposits, with a copy sent to the Registrar annually along with the Return of Deposits in Form DPT-3; a single rating obtained three years ago, with no renewal since, does not satisfy this continuing annual requirement

The second proviso to section 76(1) (and Rule 3(8)) requires the credit rating to be obtained EVERY YEAR during the tenure of the deposits, not merely at the time of the first invitation - a copy of each year's rating must be sent to the Registrar along with the Return of Deposits (Form DPT-3). Vantage's failure to renew its rating for the past three years leaves it non-compliant with this continuing obligation.

Has Sundew Pharma Limited complied with the Deposit Repayment Reserve Account requirement under section 73(2)(c) read with Rule 13, by depositing Rs. 6 crore on 25th April, 2026 against Rs. 40 crore of deposits maturing in FY 2026-27?

options.A: Yes - Rs. 6 crore exceeds 10% of Rs. 40 crore (Rs. 4 crore), and the statutory floor under Rule 13 is only 10%, not 20%, of the maturing deposit amount
options.B: No - the deposit was made too late; the statutory deadline under Rule 13 is 31st March (not 30th April) of the relevant year, so Sundew's 25th April deposit is out of time regardless of amount
options.C: Yes - Rule 13 only requires the Deposit Repayment Reserve Account to be funded to whatever extent the company's Board, in its discretion, considers adequate, with no fixed statutory percentage floor
options.D: No - although the deposit was made before the 30th April deadline, Rule 13 requires at least 20% of the maturing deposit amount (20% of Rs. 40 crore = Rs. 8 crore) to be deposited into the Deposit Repayment Reserve Account; Sundew's deposit of Rs. 6 crore falls short of this Rs. 8 crore floor, so it has not complied

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) No - although the deposit was made before the 30th April deadline, Rule 13 requires at least 20% of the maturing deposit amount (20% of Rs. 40 crore = Rs. 8 crore) to be deposited into the Deposit Repayment Reserve Account; Sundew's deposit of Rs. 6 crore falls short of this Rs. 8 crore floor, so it has not complied

Rule 13 requires at least 20% of deposits maturing in the following financial year to be deposited in the Deposit Repayment Reserve Account on or before 30th April each year. Here, 20% of Rs. 40 crore is Rs. 8 crore; Sundew's actual deposit of Rs. 6 crore (made within time, on 25th April) is short by Rs. 2 crore of the required floor, so it has NOT complied with the amount requirement, even though the timing was correct.

Can Sundew Pharma Limited accept the proposed further Rs. 5 crore in deposits from its members, given outstanding member deposits of Rs. 18 crore and an aggregate of Rs. 200 crore?

options.A: No, not in full - Rule 3(4) caps deposits from members (together with outstanding member deposits) at 10% of the Rs. 200 crore aggregate, i.e., Rs. 20 crore; with Rs. 18 crore already outstanding, only a further Rs. 2 crore (not the full Rs. 5 crore) may be accepted from members without breaching the 10% ceiling
options.B: Yes, in full - the 10% ceiling under Rule 3(4) applies only to non-member deposits, and there is no statutory ceiling at all on the amount an eligible company may accept from its own members
options.C: No, not at all - having already reached Rs. 18 crore in outstanding member deposits, Sundew has already breached the 10% ceiling and must reduce, not increase, its outstanding member deposits before accepting any further amount
options.D: Yes, in full - the applicable ceiling for member deposits of an eligible company is 35% (as for an ordinary company) rather than 10%, and 18 + 5 = Rs. 23 crore is comfortably within 35% of Rs. 200 crore (Rs. 70 crore)

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) No, not in full - Rule 3(4) caps deposits from members (together with outstanding member deposits) at 10% of the Rs. 200 crore aggregate, i.e., Rs. 20 crore; with Rs. 18 crore already outstanding, only a further Rs. 2 crore (not the full Rs. 5 crore) may be accepted from members without breaching the 10% ceiling

Rule 3(4) caps an eligible company's member deposits (including outstanding member deposits) at 10% of the aggregate of paid-up capital, free reserves, and securities premium (here, 10% of Rs. 200 crore = Rs. 20 crore) - a lower, member-specific ceiling than the 35% general ceiling under Rule 3(3), which does not apply to an eligible company's member deposits. With Rs. 18 crore already outstanding, only Rs. 2 crore of headroom remains, so Sundew may accept only Rs. 2 crore (not the full proposed Rs. 5 crore) without breaching the ceiling.

Can Sundew Pharma Limited accept the proposed further Rs. 8 crore in deposits from persons other than its members, given outstanding non-member deposits of Rs. 45 crore and an aggregate of Rs. 200 crore?

It considers three individuals: Mr. Aftab, who has no connection with Orbital Fintech or its group companies and has given his written consent to act as trustee; Mr. Baldev, who is indebted to Orbital Fintech's subsidiary company; and Ms. Chitra, who is an employee of Orbital Fintech's holding company. Separately, after the circular in the form of advertisement has already been issued and deposits accepted, Orbital Fintech's Board (which is required to have independent directors) wishes to remove the existing trustee, Mr. Devesh, midway through his term, by a resolution passed with 5 out of 9 directors present at the Board meeting voting in favour, with no independent director present at that meeting.

Is Mr. Baldev, who is indebted to Orbital Fintech's subsidiary company, eligible for appointment as a trustee for depositors?

options.A: Yes - the indebtedness disqualification under Rule 7 applies only where the person is indebted to the company itself, and indebtedness to a subsidiary, holding, or associate company does not trigger this disqualification
options.B: Yes, provided Mr. Baldev's indebtedness to the subsidiary does not exceed 10% of that subsidiary's paid-up share capital, this being the threshold below which indebtedness is disregarded under Rule 7
options.C: No - Rule 7 disqualifies a proposed trustee who is indebted to the company, or its subsidiary, holding, or associate company, or a subsidiary of such holding company; since Mr. Baldev is indebted to Orbital Fintech's subsidiary, he is disqualified from appointment as trustee for depositors
options.D: No, but only because Mr. Baldev has not furnished written consent to act as trustee; had he furnished such consent, his indebtedness to the subsidiary would not have disqualified him

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) No - Rule 7 disqualifies a proposed trustee who is indebted to the company, or its subsidiary, holding, or associate company, or a subsidiary of such holding company; since Mr. Baldev is indebted to Orbital Fintech's subsidiary, he is disqualified from appointment as trustee for depositors

Rule 7 disqualifies, among others, a person indebted to the company or its subsidiary, holding, or associate company (or a subsidiary of such holding company) from appointment as a trustee for depositors - this extends beyond indebtedness to the company itself, to indebtedness within the wider corporate group, and Mr. Baldev's indebtedness to Orbital Fintech's subsidiary squarely triggers this disqualification.

Is Ms. Chitra, an employee of Orbital Fintech's holding company, eligible for appointment as a trustee for depositors?

options.A: Yes - the employee-disqualification under Rule 7 applies only to employees of the company itself, and employment with a holding company (as distinct from the company or its subsidiary) does not trigger this disqualification
options.B: Yes, provided Ms. Chitra is not a member of Orbital Fintech's Key Managerial Personnel, this being the sole category of holding-company personnel disqualified under Rule 7
options.C: No, but only because she has not yet furnished her written consent to act as trustee; upon furnishing such consent, her employment with the holding company would no longer disqualify her
options.D: No - Rule 7 disqualifies a person who is a director, key managerial personnel, or any other officer or employee of the company OR of its holding, subsidiary, or associate company (or a depositor in the company); since Ms. Chitra is an employee of Orbital Fintech's holding company, she is disqualified from appointment as trustee

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) No - Rule 7 disqualifies a person who is a director, key managerial personnel, or any other officer or employee of the company OR of its holding, subsidiary, or associate company (or a depositor in the company); since Ms. Chitra is an employee of Orbital Fintech's holding company, she is disqualified from appointment as trustee

Rule 7 disqualifies a person who is a director, KMP, officer, or employee of the company or of its holding, subsidiary, or associate company (or is a depositor in the company) from appointment as trustee for depositors. Ms. Chitra's employment with Orbital Fintech's HOLDING company falls squarely within this disqualification, just as employment with the company itself or its subsidiary would.

Is the Board's proposed removal of Mr. Devesh (the existing trustee), by a resolution passed with 5 out of 9 directors present voting in favour and no independent director present at that meeting, valid?

options.A: No - a trustee for depositors cannot be removed from office, after the issue of the circular/advertisement and before expiry of his term, except with the consent of ALL the directors present at the Board meeting; further, since Orbital Fintech is required to have independent directors, at least one independent director must be present at that meeting - here, since no independent director was present, the removal is invalid regardless of the 5-in-favour outcome
options.B: Yes - removal of a trustee for depositors requires only a simple majority of directors present and voting at the Board meeting, exactly as for an ordinary Board resolution, with no special independent-director requirement
options.C: Yes - since 5 out of 9 directors is a majority of the total strength of the Board, this alone satisfies the 'all directors present' requirement under Rule 7, and the presence of an independent director is a mere recommendatory (not mandatory) safeguard
options.D: No, but only because the removal must additionally be approved by a special resolution of the shareholders in general meeting, a requirement independent of the directors-present condition

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) No - a trustee for depositors cannot be removed from office, after the issue of the circular/advertisement and before expiry of his term, except with the consent of ALL the directors present at the Board meeting; further, since Orbital Fintech is required to have independent directors, at least one independent director must be present at that meeting - here, since no independent director was present, the removal is invalid regardless of the 5-in-favour outcome

Rule 7 provides that no trustee for depositors shall be removed from office, after issue of the circular/advertisement and before expiry of his term, except with the CONSENT OF ALL THE DIRECTORS PRESENT at a Board meeting - and where the company is required to have independent directors, at least one independent director must be present at that meeting. Here, the resolution was passed by only 5 of the directors in favour (not necessarily all directors present) and, critically, with no independent director present at all - so the removal fails to satisfy Rule 7's safeguards.

It subsequently failed to repay the Rs. 8 crore along with interest even after the time extended by the Tribunal had expired. Separately, Ms. Priya had deposited Rs. 10 lakh with Orion Fabrics on 1st April, 2025 for a tenure of 24 months at a flat rate of interest of 9% per annum. On 1st January, 2026 - i.e., after the deposit had actually run for 9 months, which is more than six months after the date of deposit but before its actual maturity date - Ms. Priya requested premature repayment of her deposit.

What fine is Orion Fabrics Limited liable to under section 76A(a), in addition to repaying the Rs. 8 crore deposit and interest due?

options.A: A fine which shall not be less than the HIGHER of Rs. 1 crore or twice the amount of deposit accepted (i.e., Rs. 16 crore), extendable up to Rs. 10 crore, so the minimum fine payable is Rs. 16 crore
options.B: A fine which shall not be less than the LOWER of Rs. 1 crore or twice the amount of deposit accepted (i.e., twice Rs. 8 crore = Rs. 16 crore, so the lower figure is Rs. 1 crore), extendable up to Rs. 10 crore
options.C: A flat fine of exactly Rs. 10 crore in every case, irrespective of the amount of deposit accepted or contravened
options.D: A fine which shall not be less than Rs. 25 lakh, this being the officer-in-default's minimum fine mistakenly applied to the company instead

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) A fine which shall not be less than the LOWER of Rs. 1 crore or twice the amount of deposit accepted (i.e., twice Rs. 8 crore = Rs. 16 crore, so the lower figure is Rs. 1 crore), extendable up to Rs. 10 crore

Section 76A(a) fixes the company's minimum fine as the LOWER of Rs. 1 crore or twice the deposit amount accepted, extendable to Rs. 10 crore. Here, twice the deposit (Rs. 16 crore) exceeds Rs. 1 crore, so the LOWER figure - Rs. 1 crore - is the applicable statutory minimum, and the fine (as fixed by the adjudicating authority, having regard to the facts) may extend up to Rs. 10 crore, in addition to repayment of the deposit and interest due.

Given that Mr. Nakul knowingly and wilfully contravened the deposit provisions with intent to deceive the depositors, what punishment does he face under section 76A(b), and is he exposed to any further liability?

options.A: He is punishable with a fine only, of a flat Rs. 2 crore, with no provision for imprisonment and no additional liability under section 447 regardless of his intent to deceive
options.B: He is punishable with imprisonment extendable to 3 years and a fine capped at Rs. 25 lakh, and section 447 (fraud) cannot apply to an officer-in-default of a company under any circumstances
options.C: He is punishable with imprisonment extendable to 7 years and a fine of not less than Rs. 25 lakh but extendable to Rs. 2 crore under section 76A(b); and, since his contravention was knowing/wilful and intended to deceive the depositors, he is additionally liable to action under section 447 (punishment for fraud)
options.D: He is punishable exactly as the company is, i.e., with a fine which shall not be less than the lower of Rs. 1 crore or twice the deposit amount, with no separate imprisonment provision for officers

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) He is punishable with imprisonment extendable to 7 years and a fine of not less than Rs. 25 lakh but extendable to Rs. 2 crore under section 76A(b); and, since his contravention was knowing/wilful and intended to deceive the depositors, he is additionally liable to action under section 447 (punishment for fraud)

Section 76A(b) punishes the officer-in-default with imprisonment extendable to 7 years AND a fine of not less than Rs. 25 lakh but extendable to Rs. 2 crore. Where, as here, the contravention is proved to be knowing/wilful with intent to deceive the company, shareholders, depositors, creditors, or tax authorities, section 76A additionally exposes the officer to liability under section 447 (punishment for fraud) - a materially more severe exposure than the base section 76A(b) punishment alone.

At what rate of interest is Orion Fabrics Limited required to make the premature repayment to Ms. Priya, whose deposit (contracted at a flat 9% per annum) has actually run for 9 months (i.e., more than six months) before her premature-repayment request?

options.A: 9% per annum - the full contracted rate continues to apply on premature repayment made after six months have elapsed, with no reduction under Rule 15 for a deposit that has run for more than six months
options.B: 7% per annum - Rule 15 mandates a flat 2% reduction (not 1%) in the interest rate on any premature repayment made after the expiry of six months from the date of deposit
options.C: 0% per annum - Rule 15 disentitles a depositor to any interest at all where repayment is sought before the actual maturity date of the deposit, regardless of how long the deposit has already run
options.D: 8% per annum - Rule 15 requires the rate of interest payable on premature repayment (made after six months but before actual maturity) to be 1% LESS than the rate which would otherwise be payable for the period for which the deposit has actually run; since the contracted rate is a flat 9% per annum, the premature-repayment rate is 9% - 1% = 8% per annum

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) 8% per annum - Rule 15 requires the rate of interest payable on premature repayment (made after six months but before actual maturity) to be 1% LESS than the rate which would otherwise be payable for the period for which the deposit has actually run; since the contracted rate is a flat 9% per annum, the premature-repayment rate is 9% - 1% = 8% per annum

Rule 15 provides that where premature repayment is sought after six months have elapsed but before the actual maturity date, the interest rate payable shall be 1% less than the rate which would have been payable for the period the deposit has actually run. On Ms. Priya's flat 9% per annum contracted rate, this results in a premature-repayment rate of 9% - 1% = 8% per annum (the reduction does not apply where the premature repayment is to bring deposits within the Rule 3 permissible limits, or for war-risk-related benefits during an Article 352 emergency - neither of which applies here).
